articles.title: Why China’s Training Center in Laos Will Not Change Vietnam’s Non-Aligned Foreign Policy
articles.full_text:
Hanoi’s best option to keep its western neighbors neutral is to resist further Chinese encroachment by political means.
A satellite image shows the construction of the China-backed air strip in Ban Keun, Vientiane province, Laos, Jan. 3, 2026.
China’s recent announcement of the opening of a new Joint Logistics and Training Center to train air force pilots in Ban Keun, Laos, has caused much concern about China’s intentions and capabilities. The new center, together with the China-Cambodia Joint Support and Training Center at Ream Naval Base in Cambodia, gives China’s military the ability to cover inland airspace over Indochina and out toward the Gulf of Thailand.
Vietnam has not commented on the new base at Ban Keun, but Prime Minister Le Minh Hung just concluded a visit to Laos and Cambodia. Laos was Hung’s first official visit since assuming the prime ministerial post in April. Hung and Thongloun Sisoulith, the president of Laos and general secretary of the Lao People’s Revolutionary Party, affirmed the “great friendship, special solidarity, comprehensive cooperation, and strategic cohesion” between the two nations. Both countries will celebrate the 50th anniversary of the signing of the 1977 Vietnam-Laos Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation next year.
China’s new base in Laos signals one of the major developments in Indochinese affairs since 1991. The 1991 Paris Peace Agreements ended the Third Indochina War and laid the basis for how China and Vietnam would handle Indochinese affairs to avoid a repetition of the polarization and arms race that contributed to Vietnam’s invasion of Cambodia in December 1978 and China’s retaliatory invasion of Vietnam in February 1979.
The Agreements demanded the withdrawal of foreign forces and their equipment from Cambodia, thereby ending the direct Vietnamese and Chinese interference in Cambodian affairs. This agreement came two years after China and Laos had normalized ties and three years after Vietnam began to withdraw its troops from Laos. China and Vietnam normalized ties in November 1991, the month after the Paris Peace Agreements. One of the key conditions of normalization is that neither country would seek hegemony in Indochina, which was the main reason China and Vietnam fought in 1979. After 1991, neither Vietnam nor China has had a permanent military base in Laos or Cambodia.
The post-1991 status quo is now enduring a stress test with the opening of China’s joint training centers in Ream and Ban Keun. From Vietnam’s perspective, what matters is not just the current capability but China’s future intentions. Although these centers are of limited military utility, China’s military presence could polarize Indochina if Laos and Cambodia come under pressure to host more Chinese military personnel or equipment, grant China exclusive access to these centers, or give China the right to use them during wartime. If Laos and Cambodia sided with China, it would completely expose Vietnam’s western flank to a hostile foreign power.
However, Vietnam will stick to its non-aligned foreign policy (no military alliances, no siding with one country against another, no foreign military bases, and no use of force or threats to use force in international relations) to maintain its goal of keeping Laos and Cambodia neutral.
If the Third Indochina War taught Vietnam any lessons, it is that allying with a great power to keep Laos and Cambodia in its orbit is not a viable policy option. In 1977, after the Khmer Rouge attacked Vietnam with tacit Chinese support, Vietnam began to side with the Soviet Union to counter Chinese influence in Cambodia.
However, Hanoi’s decision elevated what was a local issue between China and Vietnam into a great-power rivalry between China and the Soviet Union. China could not accommodate Vietnam’s interest in Cambodia and Laos and mediate the Khmer Rouge’s conflict with Vietnam when it perceived that Vietnam was ushering a great power into China’s backyard. Such an involvement made China determined to rid Indochina of any interference by linking Vietnam’s Indochinese ambitions with Soviet “socialist imperialism.”
Beijing accused Hanoi of colonizing its western neighbors and rallied world opinion against Vietnam. Vietnam’s alliance with the Soviet Union could not help it maintain its grip on Laos and Cambodia despite Moscow bankrolling the endeavor because Chinese military and economic punishments were too severe. After the Soviet retrenchment from Indochina in 1991, the neutralization of Laos and Cambodia was inevitable.
If Vietnam hosted a foreign military base on its soil to counter China’s bases in Laos and Cambodia, this would only make China double down on its presence. The Soviet presence at Cam Ranh Bay did not end China’s support for anti-Vietnam insurgents in Laos and Cambodia. There are simply no countries that can help Vietnam compete with China over Laos and Cambodia to the degree the Soviet Union could. The United States is not a continental power in mainland Asia. As such, Hanoi cannot abandon its stance of non-alignment.
It would also not be viable for Vietnam to threaten to attack China’s bases in Laos and Cambodia. This is not the first time China set up a joint training center in either Laos or Cambodia. In 1977, China helped the Khmer Rouge construct the 2,400-meter-long Krang Leav airfield in Kampong Chhnang, which at the time would allow China to station short-range bombers to carry out raids in southern Vietnam. China trained Khmer Rouge pilots and pledged to donate fifty-six aircraft to Cambodia. China also stationed engineering troops to construct roads in northern Laos beginning in 1962.
When Vietnam invaded Cambodia in December 1978, it quickly captured the unfinished Krang Leav airfield, thereby ending the Chinese threat from the southwestern front. Hanoi also captured Kampong Som (Sihanoukville), Cambodia’s only major seaport, through which it received Chinese war material. Although China did not send troops to Cambodia, Vietnam’s use of force against Cambodia gave Beijing the pretext to launch a retaliatory attack in February 1979. Laos subsequently ceased all cooperation with China, ending China’s military presence in Laos, but it did not restrain Beijing’s military punishment of Vietnam along the China-Vietnam land border and in the South China Sea.
It is not hard to imagine that Vietnam’s decision to use force against Ban Keun and Ream in the future would result in another Chinese attack. Vietnam can use long-range missiles to attack Chinese bases in Laos and Cambodia, which can spare the country of an invasion and limit escalation. However, there is no guarantee that China would not launch missiles against Vietnam’s bases or maritime outposts.
Because Vietnam can neither arms race nor side with a great power against China, Vietnam’s best option to keep Laos and Cambodia neutral is to resist further Chinese presence by political means. Vietnam’s friendship treaty with Laos should provide some degree of consultation between the two countries, as the treaty commits both countries to come to the defense of the other. Laos being transparent with Vietnam over the extent of Chinese presence and any future expansion plans would allay Hanoi’s fear to some degree. Vietnam’s affirmation of the 1991 Paris Peace Agreements and Cambodia’s constitutional clauses barring foreign bases from Cambodian soil remain vital. Like Laos’ case, Vietnam should press for more transparency over China’s presence at Ream. Vietnam should also highlight the continued trilateral cooperation framework among the three Indochinese countries to lock in the economic and political benefits of them cooperating with rather than siding against Vietnam.
Besides direct approaches toward its western neighbors, Vietnam can dilute the significance of Chinese centers by supporting more foreign presences there. The Ream Naval Base is a case in point. Although China funded the renovation and expansion of the base, Cambodia has invited foreign warships from Vietnam, Japan, the United States, Australia, India, and others to visit the base. If China’s center in Ban Keun is not directed against any third party, foreign countries should seek regular access to the center to refuel aircraft or exchange technical expertise with the Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force. Vietnam’s diversified foreign policy means that it doesn’t matter which country visits the center, just that no countries are excluded from stopping at Ban Keun. This is how Vietnam’s foreign partners can help it achieve its objectives in western Indochina without alarming China.
Finally, Vietnam keeping its relationship with China amicable is the best method of keeping Laos and Cambodia neutral. Some observers have argued that the new bases in Laos and Cambodia signal a failure of Hanoi’s China policy. Despite Vietnam joining China’s “Community of Common Destiny” in 2023, these analysts claim, China is continuing the “encirclement” of Vietnam. However, this assessment downplays China’s largely non-confrontational stance toward Vietnam’s land reclamation campaign at sea. It is also worth noting that China calls the two facilities joint centers and not exclusive military bases, which signals a desire on Beijing’s part not to provoke Hanoi. Importantly, it is China’s air force and the navy that are at those bases and not the army, which would be more threatening to Vietnam. China has an interest in keeping its undisputed southern border with Vietnam stable while it focuses on Taiwan. In exchange, Vietnam must continue assuring China that it has no intention of siding with another great power against it. Such an assurance deprives China of any rationale to turn Laos and Cambodia against Vietnam.
The post-1991 Indochina order is now being tested, but many facets of that order are worth preserving. Vietnam’s and China’s reciprocal commitment not to establish permanent foreign bases in Laos and Cambodia and not to seek hegemony over Indochina will prevent the peninsula from being plunged into another China-Vietnam conflict or a conflict between China and Vietnam’s great power ally. So long as China’s presence in Laos and Cambodia does not result in them turning against Vietnam, Vietnam will continue honoring the post-1991 order.
China’s recent announcement of the opening of a new Joint Logistics and Training Center to train air force pilots in Ban Keun, Laos, has caused much concern about China’s intentions and capabilities. The new center, together with the China-Cambodia Joint Support and Training Center at Ream Naval Base in Cambodia, gives China’s military the ability to cover inland airspace over Indochina and out toward the Gulf of Thailand.
Vietnam has not commented on the new base at Ban Keun, but Prime Minister Le Minh Hung just concluded a visit to Laos and Cambodia. Laos was Hung’s first official visit since assuming the prime ministerial post in April. Hung and Thongloun Sisoulith, the president of Laos and general secretary of the Lao People’s Revolutionary Party, affirmed the “great friendship, special solidarity, comprehensive cooperation, and strategic cohesion” between the two nations. Both countries will celebrate the 50th anniversary of the signing of the 1977 Vietnam-Laos Treaty of Friendship and Cooperation next year.
China’s new base in Laos signals one of the major developments in Indochinese affairs since 1991. The 1991 Paris Peace Agreements ended the Third Indochina War and laid the basis for how China and Vietnam would handle Indochinese affairs to avoid a repetition of the polarization and arms race that contributed to Vietnam’s invasion of Cambodia in December 1978 and China’s retaliatory invasion of Vietnam in February 1979.
The Agreements demanded the withdrawal of foreign forces and their equipment from Cambodia, thereby ending the direct Vietnamese and Chinese interference in Cambodian affairs. This agreement came two years after China and Laos had normalized ties and three years after Vietnam began to withdraw its troops from Laos. China and Vietnam normalized ties in November 1991, the month after the Paris Peace Agreements. One of the key conditions of normalization is that neither country would seek hegemony in Indochina, which was the main reason China and Vietnam fought in 1979. After 1991, neither Vietnam nor China has had a permanent military base in Laos or Cambodia.
The post-1991 status quo is now enduring a stress test with the opening of China’s joint training centers in Ream and Ban Keun. From Vietnam’s perspective, what matters is not just the current capability but China’s future intentions. Although these centers are of limited military utility, China’s military presence could polarize Indochina if Laos and Cambodia come under pressure to host more Chinese military personnel or equipment, grant China exclusive access to these centers, or give China the right to use them during wartime. If Laos and Cambodia sided with China, it would completely expose Vietnam’s western flank to a hostile foreign power.
However, Vietnam will stick to its non-aligned foreign policy (no military alliances, no siding with one country against another, no foreign military bases, and no use of force or threats to use force in international relations) to maintain its goal of keeping Laos and Cambodia neutral.
If the Third Indochina War taught Vietnam any lessons, it is that allying with a great power to keep Laos and Cambodia in its orbit is not a viable policy option. In 1977, after the Khmer Rouge attacked Vietnam with tacit Chinese support, Vietnam began to side with the Soviet Union to counter Chinese influence in Cambodia.
However, Hanoi’s decision elevated what was a local issue between China and Vietnam into a great-power rivalry between China and the Soviet Union. China could not accommodate Vietnam’s interest in Cambodia and Laos and mediate the Khmer Rouge’s conflict with Vietnam when it perceived that Vietnam was ushering a great power into China’s backyard. Such an involvement made China determined to rid Indochina of any interference by linking Vietnam’s Indochinese ambitions with Soviet “socialist imperialism.”
Beijing accused Hanoi of colonizing its western neighbors and rallied world opinion against Vietnam. Vietnam’s alliance with the Soviet Union could not help it maintain its grip on Laos and Cambodia despite Moscow bankrolling the endeavor because Chinese military and economic punishments were too severe. After the Soviet retrenchment from Indochina in 1991, the neutralization of Laos and Cambodia was inevitable.
If Vietnam hosted a foreign military base on its soil to counter China’s bases in Laos and Cambodia, this would only make China double down on its presence. The Soviet presence at Cam Ranh Bay did not end China’s support for anti-Vietnam insurgents in Laos and Cambodia. There are simply no countries that can help Vietnam compete with China over Laos and Cambodia to the degree the Soviet Union could. The United States is not a continental power in mainland Asia. As such, Hanoi cannot abandon its stance of non-alignment.
It would also not be viable for Vietnam to threaten to attack China’s bases in Laos and Cambodia. This is not the first time China set up a joint training center in either Laos or Cambodia. In 1977, China helped the Khmer Rouge construct the 2,400-meter-long Krang Leav airfield in Kampong Chhnang, which at the time would allow China to station short-range bombers to carry out raids in southern Vietnam. China trained Khmer Rouge pilots and pledged to donate fifty-six aircraft to Cambodia. China also stationed engineering troops to construct roads in northern Laos beginning in 1962.
articles.summary: Hanoi's best option to keep its western neighbors neutral is to resist further Chinese encroachment by political means.

articles.title: Malaysia to Raise Transboundary Haze Crisis With ASEAN Foreign Ministers Ahead of Summit
articles.full_text:
This year’s particularly severe haze season has once again exposed the void in national and regional efforts to combat the problem.
Thick haze obscures the sky above a residential area in Kalimantan, Indonesia, Aug. 20, 2026.
Malaysia’s government will raise the issue of transboundary haze at an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) foreign ministers’ meeting ahead of the bloc’s 49th Summit in Manila next month.
Over the past four months, massive wildfires have raged across Indonesia, particularly on the islands of Borneo and Sumatra, causing a toxic haze that has seriously impacted Malaysia, Brunei, Singapore, and parts of the Philippines.
Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan told reporters in Sepang yesterday that the haze issue required special attention as it was not covered by existing ASEAN mechanisms for natural disasters, the state media agency Bernama reported.
“We already have an ASEAN mechanism for natural disasters, but haze is not included or classified as a natural disaster,” he said. “So, this will be one of the issues that I will personally raise at the meeting with my counterparts.”
Air pollution from the fires, which have been prolonged and exacerbated by an unusually severe dry season, has forced the closure of schools across Malaysia in recent weeks. Last week, the government ordered schools to close in Melaka, Negri Sembilan, Selangor, Kuala Lumpur, and Putrajaya due to the worsening haze. The Malaysian capital rated among the world’s most polluted major cities globally. This came after hundreds of schools across the state of Sarawak on Borneo shut last month due to the hazardous air pollution in neighboring Kalimantan.
Malaysia has already been in touch with the Indonesian authorities about the fires. Last week, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said that he had discussed the situation with Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, who had “agreed to take the necessary steps.”
Mohamad Hasan said yesterday that Indonesia’s new foreign minister Arrmanatha Nasir had informed him that poor visibility in affected areas was hampering aerial firefighting operations. Many of the fires were also located deep inland, where water supplies were limited, and that some were in peatland areas, where fire-fighting is particularly challenging.
“Indonesia has between three to four aeroplanes and 34 helicopters, but they cannot take off because visibility is so poor that it is unsafe for any flights in the affected areas,” he said, as per Bernama.
Rizal Irawan, a senior official at Indonesia’s Environment Ministry, said last month that the country’s authorities were investigating 19 companies that it believes may be linked to the wildfires, and said it would investigate who might be responsible. Whether or not these investigations result in prosecutions and punishments remains to be seen.
“Transboundary haze” has become a seasonal crisis in large parts of Southeast Asia, much of it caused by agricultural burn-off on monoculture plantations, including palm oil, maize, paper pulp, and sugar. These are compounded by vehicle and industrial emissions and naturally occurring dry season forest fires.
This year’s particularly prolonged haze season has once again exposed the void in national and regional efforts to combat the problem. Some nations have introduced their own legislation to tackle the haze problem, but effective enforcement requires support from the nation where the fires are located, something which has not always been forthcoming.
In 2002, ASEAN member states signed the ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution (AATHP), a recognition of the need “to co-ordinate national action for preventing and monitoring transboundary haze pollution.” In April, the 11-nation bloc inaugurated the ASEAN Coordinating Center for Transboundary Haze Pollution Control in Jakarta, which reflects member states’ “shared determination to achieve a haze-free region through stronger cooperation and faster response,” as Environment Minister Hanif Faisol Nurofiq put it at the time.
Much like the bloc’s human rights instruments, however, the AATHP and other ASEAN mechanisms are weighted heavily toward consensus and national sovereignty. As Rizky Ihsan of Griffith University put it in a recent article, “rather than restricting the states that signed up to it, the AATHP was designed to be acceptable to them.” Under the agreement, Rizky argued, “national governments have considerable control over how problems are reported, how emergencies are defined, and when outside help is requested.” He noted that similar issues also apply to the new Coordinating Center, which “will assist only when the national authority declares an emergency and asks for help.”
ASEAN is clearly aware that more effective regional mechanisms are necessary to combat the problem. Further discussions at next month’s ASEAN Summit to this end could be a welcome, if belated, move in this direction.
The challenge is that it not only requires cooperation between nations that often jealously guard their own sovereign prerogatives; it also, in many cases, requires confrontations with entrenched business interests that are unpalatable for national governments, and likely very challenging for regional mechanisms. Without serious coordination and a willingness to cede a degree of sovereignty in the service of the regional interest, Southeast Asia’s annual haze problem is only likely to continue.

articles.title: Philippine Lower House Passes Bill Restricting Social Media Access of Minors
articles.full_text:
If passed into law, the country will become the fourth in Southeast Asia to introduce youth social media restrictions of some kind.
The Philippine House of Representatives yesterday approved a measure barring children under the age of 13 from social media. It has become the latest nation in Southeast Asia to tighten online safety provisions for minors.
The Safe and Friendly Environment for Kids in Digital Spaces Act was passed nearly unanimously, with 287 lawmakers voting in favor and three against, Inquirer.net reported.
The measures align the Philippines with a growing global effort to restrict minors’ access to social media platforms, in the interests of protecting them from cyberbullying, online fraud, and exposure to pornography, among other perceived threats.
In the Philippines, the legislative push has come after a string of incidents of school violence that the government believes were driven by online content. Last month, a 16-year-old shot dead two fellow students and injured eight others at a school in the southern Philippines, before taking his own life.
This followed a similar incident in the same region in August, in which a student at a Catholic school live-streamed himself shooting and killing ​a classmate before taking his own life. Also in June, two students shot and killed three and injured seven of their peers at a school in Tacloban, allegedly in response to bullying.
Under the proposed bill, children aged 13 and below would be prohibited from creating social media accounts. Meanwhile, a variety of restrictions would be put in place for those under 18 years of age. They will be barred from making online purchases and engaging with “gambling-like mechanisms” and other features that may pose “reasonably foreseeable and material risks” to their well-being. They would also be shielded from harmful ads and algorithmic short-video feeds that encourage limitless scrolling, according to Inquirer.net.
Filipinos are heavy users of social media. The country has the sixth-largest pool of Facebook users in the world, with more than 102 million accounts registered, and an estimated 78.1 million TikTok accounts, the seventh-largest of any country. According to research, Filipinos spend an average of nearly 34 hours per week on social media.
Yesterday’s vote came after ⁠the Senate’s recent endorsement of a similar but slightly stricter bill, which would ban a minor under 18 years of age from registering, accessing, using, or maintaining an account on any age-restricted social media platform. According to Inquirer.net, the two dueling bills are now set for a “legislative showdown,” and it remains to be seen exactly what the final version of the legislation will look like.
These moves follow Australia’s introduction of the world’s first social media ban for under 16s. The policy, which took effect in December of last year, forces social media firms to block users under 16 from having accounts on their platforms, rather than penalizing young people or their parents. Despite the lingering questions about the effectiveness of such restrictions, a long list of countries, including India, China, Türkiye, the United Kingdom, the European Union, and several in Europe, have since followed suit and announced the introduction of curbs of some kind.
Within Southeast Asia, Indonesia in March became the first nation to ban under-16s from having accounts on what it termed “high-risk” digital platforms, including YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, Threads, X, Bigo Live, and Roblox. Malaysia started enforcing a similar ban on June 1, and ordered major social media platforms to conduct ​age verification against government-issued records. It has given them until January to ​implement the ⁠measure.
Vietnam also announced in July that it planned to introduce social media restrictions for minors. While Hanoi will not ban minors’ access to social media platforms, the new rules would bar under 16s from posting, commenting, sharing, or reacting to posts on social media.

articles.title: Wolf Warriors in Sheep’s Clothing: China’s New Subnational Diplomacy in Australia
articles.full_text:
Beijing’s diplomatic officials are adopting the language of the Albanese government to press their demands upon local governments and communities.
For the government of China, diplomacy is more than simply a means of cultivating international relationships and advancing national interests. It is also an instrument of regime maintenance. In this capacity it can take the form of coercive interventions in the domestic affairs of other states with the aim of suppressing conduct or critique considered hostile to the ruling Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Deploying diplomatic agents to secure compliance with CCP objectives is in fact a significant feature of China’s subnational relations with local governments and communities in Australia.
During Xi Jinping’s first decade as CCP general secretary and chairman of state, Beijing’s approach to Australia grew increasingly blunt and confrontational, a style known as “wolf warrior diplomacy.” More recently, Chinese diplomats have shifted to a quieter, more self-assured form of subnational diplomacy. In contrast to the bluster of the wolf warrior era, this approach is largely conducted behind closed doors and has become more evident since Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s July 2025 visit to China.
The election of the Albanese government in 2022 early signaled a thaw in what had been an icy bilateral relationship between Australia and China under the preceding Coalition governments of Malcolm Turnbull (2015-18) and Scott Morrison (2018-22).  On his second visit to China as prime minister, Albanese spent a week “stabilizing” relations through renewed business, trade, educational, cultural, and inter-governmental initiatives.  
Among the knock-on effects in Australia was a flurry of Chinese diplomatic initiatives at the local level. Consular staff in Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide, and Perth now plainly assumed they were licensed by Albanese and his business entourage to press for local Australian compliance with their own demands on a range of issues. In meetings with local governments and peak community bodies, they carried a message: tolerating comments or events that displeased or offended the Chinese state or CCP would embarrass not just China or its ruling party, but the government of Australia. 
This was new. Rather than howling into the void, China’s diplomats were framing their demands in the Australian government’s own idiom. Wolf warrior diplomacy was giving way to “wolf warrior in sheep’s clothing diplomacy.” China’s officials were adopting the language of their hosts to press their demands upon local governments and communities. On evidence, to date the new approach is relatively effective but it carries risks for all parties.
A consular initiative in Melbourne undertaken shortly after the conclusion of Albanese’s trip to China shows the strategy in action.  In August 2025, China’s consul general in Melbourne requested a meeting with an independent non-profit organization that will remain unnamed. Its board welcomed the approach. This was not a low-key visit. The cluster of consular colleagues accompanying the consul general almost outnumbered the hosts around the table. 
During the formal presentation, the consul general reviewed Australia-China ties since 1972 and Melbourne’s consular opening in 1986. Past difficulties were behind us, he said. The Albanese government had corrected the errors of its Coalition predecessor. Canberra was restoring stability through trade, regional development, and people-to-people partnerships while recognizing China’s core interests – code for CCP rule and China’s claims over Taiwan, Tibet, Xinjiang, and the South China Sea, among other claims. 
The consul general then urged the board to read a recent article by iron-ore tycoon Andrew (Twiggy) Forrest, who predicted a bright future if everyone came on board the China boat. But, Forrest also warned: “Treat a friend like an enemy, and one day they may well become one.”  
A few locals around the table recalled hearing a similar warning five years earlier, when a Chinese diplomat presented a Canberra journalist with a list of 14 grievances, accompanied by the statement: “If you make China the enemy, China will be the enemy.” Most of those grievances presented in November 2020 concerned Canberra’s efforts to limit Chinese government engagement with subnational entities, on the one hand, and its failure to restrict independent Australian institutions critical of China and the CCP on the other.  China’s representatives in Australia appeared to be agitated not so much by the Coalition government’s external relations as by its domestic political arrangements governing the states and its failure to suppress commentary on China and its ruling party in Australia’s media, think tanks, and civil society.  
The public backlash to the “14 grievances” prompted China’s local representatives to park their threat for the time being. Events proved that they could afford to wait because the same warning would be reiterated by Forrest, one of Australia’s leading businessmen, in wake of Albanese’s visit.  
Having invoked Forrest, consular officials came up with a pointed request for the Melbourne board to cancel an event it was hosting with Australian journalist Cheng Lei. Cheng had been recently repatriated following three years in a Chinese jail for alleged spying activities. Giving her a platform to discuss her imprisonment, the Chinese diplomats implied, would undo all the good work of Albanese and his business team.
Despite the consul general’s request, Cheng’s talk went ahead. Nonetheless, China’s coercive interventions around her activities continued. Six months later, her play “1154 Days,” which recounted her solitary confinement and imprisonment in China, was dropped from Melbourne’s premier arts festival. “I feel like I’m back in China,” Cheng Lei told The Age.
Her concern was justified. The play had received a provisional place on the arts festival program, normally a routine step toward inclusion, but the board – not the festival’s creative staff – ruled against it. The RISING arts festival is funded through Creative Victoria and managed through the City of Melbourne’s Arts House, placing the festival program in a classic pincer movement between state and city governments known for their habit of surrender under consular pressure. 
Chinese government meddling in Victoria’s school textbooks, community organizations, Chinese-language media, and local government deliberations had been thought things of the past following the introduction of new federal laws around foreign interference in 2018 and legislation limiting state government overreach in foreign relations in 2020. Not so. 
Interviewed for this article, Cheng said that City of Melbourne officials received several consular calls and a personal visit urging them to avoid her play. Some did resist the pressure and attended. Arts House, for its part, was supportive of the work and kept the dates even though it wasn’t part of the RISING festival. The problem was not costs but the risks to the city and state governments’ relations with the local consulate
Cheng’s play was performed off-festival with support from a venue outside the City of Melbourne’s jurisdiction. There is a curious historical parallel here. In 1936 an anti-Nazi play was banned from city theaters in Sydney and Melbourne following representations from the German consulate, then under the direction of the Nazi Party. To their credit, the players found a way around the ban by performing on the back of a truck. 
For the fleet of Chinese consuls sailing in the wake of Albanese’s China visit, Melbourne was just one port of call. The Victorian consular team sought meetings with civic institutions and officials in Bendigo, Ballarat, Frankston, Geelong, and also Hobart in Tasmania, as well as with university executives and cultural institutions, including Melbourne’s Museum of Chinese Australian History. Consular officials based in Western Australia met up with local government officers in Perth, Joondalup, Cockburn, Gosnells, Geraldton, and Swan; Queensland-based ones visited Brisbane, Rockhampton, Mackay, Toowoomba, the Sunshine Coast, Gold Coast, and Southern Downs. The South Australian consulate paid visits to the local governments of Adelaide, Murray Bridge, and Clare Valley. In each state, consular officials also met with civic and community bodies.
In contrast to earlier consular tours, the nationwide consular outreach following Albanese’s visit drew little public attention. Not long beforehand, the Sydney consular team suffered public embarrassment when local newspapers reported on the consul general’s meeting with the mayor of Newcastle. At that meeting, the consul warned the mayor against the possibility of an AUKUS nuclear-submarine squadron possibly being based nearby, saying that this would harm China’s strategic interests. The mayor was reportedly taken aback to have been challenged on Taiwan, Tibet, and nuclear submarines – topics well outside the scope of Australian local government diplomacy – during a routine meet-and-greet with Chinese consular officials.
On Albanese’s return, consular teams adopted a quieter subnational style aligned with Canberra’s own “calm and measured” international diplomacy, which was explicitly contrasted with the former Coalition’s “bellicose megaphone diplomacy.”  Albanese’s approach, while helping to restore bilateral commercial, ministerial, and people-to-people ties at the national level, raised expectations on the part of China’s representatives in Australia that their demands for local discretion on sensitive matters would yield willing compliance. Canberra’s restraint was being repurposed to serve Beijing’s coercive subnational diplomacy.
It is doubtless clear to China’s diplomats in Australia that the Albanese government’s measured diplomacy has not altered Australia’s broader strategy in the region. This geopolitical strategy was inherited intact from the Coalition government and is aligned with regional partners’ understanding of the challenges and threats China presents.
That does not inhibit consular officials from cajoling local governments and community organizations to silence talk of those threats in the interests of stabilizing bilateral relations. In May 2026, Melbourne’s consul general told a local city newspaper that claims of “so-called” threats would “backfire” and rebound “just like a boomerang” on any making them. 
Backfire on whom? Most consular interventions have remained below Canberra’s threshold of awareness, but this is changing. In July 2026, Melbourne’s Museum of Chinese Australian History appeared to breach a federal funding agreement by hosting a consular speaker at its annual high-achievers program without notifying the government funding body. The rotating host for the 2026 Chinese Australian Achievers Awards was Lord Mayor Nicholas Reece of the City of Melbourne, which customarily invites China’s consular officials to speak at community events. By withdrawing funding, Canberra signaled its concern about consular officials piggybacking at federal expense on local events.
A more serious threshold was crossed later that month when the Museum first invited then disinvited Foreign Minister Penny Wong to launch journalist Emilia Tagaza’s book “Behind a Million Faces,” described by the Museum as “a seminal book on the history of Chinese Australians.” Wong accepted the invitation. Her office nominated September 1, 2026 for the launch, and it requested an advance copy of the book to be forwarded ahead of that date. 
In July, however, according to emails reviewed by the author, members of the Museum board reviewed their own advance copies and objected to its contents on several grounds. These included the author allegedly underplaying the U.S. factor in Australia’s deteriorating relations with China and overemphasizing communism, exaggerating China’s “assertiveness,” and incorrectly suggesting that Chinese migrants to Australia sought to escape CCP control. It directed the CEO to forward the author 17 pages of corrections, none of a factual nature, most entailing reframing  the agreed facts to minimize offense to the government of China. When Tagaza rejected the board’s amendments, the CEO was directed to cancel the launch and withdraw the invitation to the foreign minister.
That was not the end of it. The CEO reinstated the launch and Wong’s invitation after receiving advice that the board decision may have infringed the author’s free speech. Just weeks before the event, however, the board again reversed course and canceled the event and the invitation. September passed without the Museum book launch, and with the foreign minister wondering what on earth was happening in Melbourne.  
She had more than one reason to wonder. In 2024 a former Museum board member had become the first Australian to be jailed for planning foreign interference on behalf of the CCP – although not in his role on the board. But in fact nothing out of the ordinary was happening in Melbourne. Conspicuous displays of anticipatory obedience toward the local consulate are the default position among state and city governments, elite cultural institutions, and peak organizations in the city.  Given sufficient haranguing and inducement, institutions adapt their behavior to what they imagine local consuls want, in many cases without receiving specific requests. Self-censorship is commonplace.
The Museum too has a record of silencing voices and histories that could annoy China’s local officials. A small everyday instance of anticipatory obedience can be found in the Museum’s display on the recent history of immigration from China. A Museum volunteer told me that a draft text linked the 1989 Beijing/Tiananmen Massacre to Prime Minister Bob Hawke’s memorable offer of permanent residence after the massacre to tens of thousands of resident Chinese students. Were it not for the Chinese military’s slaughter of students and workers in Beijing, the 40,000 students would not have been invited to stay. The text on display elides this “offensive” context: “40,000 students arrived and studied whilst many stayed in Australia.”
More seriously, the Museum promotes certain histories while silencing others. The board raised no concerns before or after the launch in August 2026 of a book on the history of the Victorian branch of the Australia-China Friendship Society (ACFS), held at the Museum in association with events marking the 75th anniversary of that Society’s founding. The ACFS’s relationship with China is mediated by the Chinese People’s Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries under the direction of the CCP’s United Front Work Department. The consul general spoke at the historical commemoration along with Lord Mayor Nicholas Reece.  
What was novel in the case of Tagaza’s aborted book launch was not the selective censorship but censorship undertaken in full gaze of the Australian foreign minister. The board’s customary deference to China’s official perspectives on Australian history, immigration, and bilateral relations is not normally acted out in front of federal ministers. And this time the coercive influence over local government and community affairs wielded by China’s consulate in Melbourne embarrassed a senior member of Albanese’s Cabinet.
articles.summary: Beijing’s diplomatic officials are adopting the language of the Albanese government to press their demands upon local governments and communities.

articles.title: What the US and China Should Discuss at APEC
articles.full_text:
Both sides are feeding an AI investment bubble – and Shenzhen is the place to talk about it.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump shake hands during their summit at the White House, Sep. 24, 2026.
On September 24, the presidents of the United States and China met in Washington and agreed to build what their joint language calls a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” On November 18-19, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet again, on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen. Two summits in three months is a rare occurrence in China-U.S. relations. 
In the September summit, already their second of 2026, one key area stood out as the focus: artificial intelligence. The risks of AI now have a dedicated channel for discussion. There’s not yet a corresponding China-U.S. platform for talking about the economics of the AI race. 
During Trump’s state visit to Beijing in May, the two leaders agreed to restart government-to-government AI dialogue. In September, at the eighth round of economic consultations in New York and Washington, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng held the first AI dialogue within that framework. They agreed to establish a channel for communications on AI incidents, and scheduled a second round of talks before the end of November. 
Shortly thereafter, at the presidential summit, Xi described China and the United States as two AI powers that should “draw on each other’s strengths, not guard against each other.” He added, “The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI.” Trump noted that discussions on “pressing issues” related to (among other topics) AI, which he calls “superintelligence,” could “promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come.” Both leaders thus offered the new dialogue platform political cover.
That is genuine progress, with a revealing limit. All the steps thus far – the exchanges on risks and benefits, the incident channel, the push for lab self-regulation – concern the dangers AI might create. Nothing yet addresses the looming economic problem of the AI sector. 
In the United States, recent developments are rather worrying. The business model for U.S. frontier AI businesses assumes that compute demand will keep growing exponentially, model capability will convert reliably into revenue, and capital will stay patient. All three assumptions are looking increasingly risky. 
The capex needed to remain at the frontier is heavier, relative to the industry’s age, than anything technology has carried before. Utilities are signing power contracts for gigawatts of capacity that do not exist. 
Meanwhile, Wall Street has started asking a question it ignored a year ago: where, exactly, is the return? In July, efficient Chinese open-weight models showed that frontier-level performance could be reached with a fraction of the compute. AI-linked U.S. equities sold off hard; analysts stepped back from price targets built on the assumption of permanent scarcity. 
China has the mirror-image problem. Chinese companies are trying to close the frontier gap under foreign constraints while having to produce returns large enough to justify the spending at home. In a September study, the Rhodium Group calculated that the combined free cash flow of Chinese tech giants Alibaba, Tencent, and Baidu swung from positive 170 billion yuan in 2025 to negative 16 billion yuan in the first half of 2026. 
The five American hyperscalers saw their own fall from $191 billion to $14 billion and raised $163 billion in long-term debt in six months to keep building. 
Clearly, neither the U.S. nor the Chinese AI sector can fund this race from operations anymore. Both countries’ capital markets are tired of narratives without actual returns. Patience on both sides is wearing thin.
The China-U.S. competition exacerbates these economic dynamics. Each new round of U.S. export controls accelerates the Chinese substitution process, which shrinks the market available for American firms. At the same time, deeper substitution raises the investment China must absorb, which worsens China’s return-on-capital problem. 
In other words, further escalation in the AI race might drain away the capital both systems depends on. This is not a moral argument, but a real financial dilemma. 
Washington and Beijing have already conceded, in their September dialogue, that they face some common risks from AI risks. What’s not clear is whether the economic problem is included on that agenda. 
The November APEC summit offers an unusually practical setting for addressing this issue. The APEC CEO Summit will bring about 1,000 business leaders to Shenzhen with AI on the formal agenda and a Shenzhen Initiative to be released. The host city itself, long nicknamed the Silicon Valley of the East, holds China’s densest cluster of AI and robotics firms. 
Unofficial channels are also in place. Tsinghua’s Center for International Security and Strategy and the Brookings Institution have hosted 14 rounds of China-U.S. AI dialogue since 2019, with Microsoft’s former chief research and strategy officer Craig Mundie serving as a co-chair. 
Three deliverables should be on the agenda for the APEC meeting.
First, China and the United States should add the missing piece of the puzzle in Shenzhen. The official AI dialogue will be held in November; at the APEC summit, both sides can start a standing China-U.S. AI economics dialogue mechanism supported by think tanks and industry associations, the “track two” format long used in China-U.S. exchanges. 
Every official AI conversation so far lacks the people who control the money: finance officials, stock market regulators, and executives. The first such dialogue could take place on the margins of the APEC meeting, convened by think tanks and industry associations rather than ministries. 
In Shenzhen, the Guangdong Artificial Intelligence Industry Association – which operates the Guangdong AI & Robotics Overseas Service Center, the province’s platform for firms going global – could co-convene, alongside established think tanks, a working session between U.S. investors, analysts, and executives and their Guangdong counterparts, on the industry’s own ground. 
Why start with the “track two” format? Because the U.S. and Chinese governments would find it hard to host this conversation. No U.S. administration can openly entertain the thought that its AI boom may be overextended; no Chinese ministry can candidly compare burn rates with a foreign power. Finance officials can talk to economists, and economists can talk to each other. An unofficial venue is the only why this particular talk can happen. 
Second, China and the United States should set a floor under export controls and market access in Shenzhen. Neither side can afford to be seen conducting negotiations over such fundamental issues, but they can quietly exchange red lines in a private setting. Misjudgment, not malice, triggers most crises. The cheapest deterrent is a sentence spoken early. 
Third, it’s time to increase collaborations on the periphery. Standards for AI deployment in third countries – things like data governance, safety evaluation, labor displacement – don’t always pit U.S. and Chinese interests against each other. In fact, that happens far less often than either side assumes. Shenzhen has already hosted APEC-track discussions on responsible AI under the Policy Partnership on Science, Technology and Innovation framework. A joint signal from Washington and Beijing supporting shared regional norms would cost little, match the CEO Summit’s own agenda, and keep third parties from profiting from dueling standards. 
By greenlighting discussions on the economic side of AI, Washington would be shifting a burden, not making a concession. Industry leaders and academic would be the interlocutors, meaning the administration does not need to make more promises even while the Treasury gains more insight into AI’s financial stability.
For its part, Beijing would reinforce its longstanding claim that Chinese AI is an economic project rather than a military one. The talks would also give China’s capital-hungry sector a forum to argue against escalation using commercial – not diplomatic – logic.
The dialogue wouldn’t release a communiqué or joint statement. This would be a recurring conversation that, over time, builds a shared vocabulary for what sustainable AI competition could look like. 
The capital markets are not waiting; they are repricing both countries’ AI sectors now. There’s still a chance for China and the U.S. to get ahead of the bubble, but the window is closing. After the U.S. midterms, coalition politics in Washington will harden, and every unmanaged month afterwards would strengthen the case for constraint in Beijing.
On September 24, the presidents of the United States and China met in Washington and agreed to build what their joint language calls a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” On November 18-19, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet again, on the sidelines of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen. Two summits in three months is a rare occurrence in China-U.S. relations.
articles.summary: Both sides are feeding an AI investment bubble – and Shenzhen is the place to talk about it.

articles.title: The Mystery of Kyrgyzstan’s Newly Launched Satellite(s)
articles.full_text:
At first glance, the story of Kyrgyzstan’s satellite launch seemed like a genuine achievement. Then the story changed.
Image of Kyrgyzstan’s unnamed, loaf-of-bread-sized nanosatellite.
On October 1, Kyrgyzstan reportedly joined Central Asia’s other spacefaring nations, successfully launching a domestically designed and produced nanosatellite aboard a SpaceX rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California
According to Kyrgyzstan’s government, the unnamed, loaf-of-bread-sized spacecraft weighs 5 kilograms, cost around $130,0000, was equipped with high-resolution cameras, and was — nearly exclusively — the product of domestic innovation. 
The satellite was assembled by two local companies, Kyrgyz Asman and Kyrgyz Electronics, Bishkek stated. The latter company’s director Ilya Cherny did admit that the technology behind the satellite was largely Russian, but pointed out that the team behind its production consisted of 10 homegrown engineers. 
The government also said the satellite would help advance Kyrgyzstan’s top agricultural, environmental, and strategic priorities over its purported 15-year lifespan.
In a statement published on September 24, the country’s Ministry of Water Resources, Agriculture and Processing Industry stated the satellite’s data would track crop conditions, detect early signs of drought, and monitor glaciers.
Speaking from California on launch day, Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov said that the country had previously had to pay to obtain this kind of data from other countries, no matter whether it was “information on 100 hectares, 1,000 hectares, or the weather.”
Japarov suggested that the satellite would allow “every square meter” of Kyrgyzstan’s land to be studied to determine its potential arability, while touting the launch as an achievement in national self-sufficiency.
“We did not have our own satellite before… now we will no longer be dependent on [other countries],” Japarov added. “We will control it ourselves 100 percent from Bishkek.”
At first glance, the story of Kyrgyzstan’s satellite launch seemed like a genuine achievement. The country had joined Kazakhstan, Turkmenistan, and – as of this August – Uzbekistan in the ranks of Central Asia’s spacefarers, largely thanks to its own ingenuity.
The success had been extensively covered in domestic, regional, and international media. And then came a confusing development. 
On October 2, the day after launch, news reports began to include a previously unmentioned detail: the satellite was a joint effort between Kyrgyzstan and the United Arab Emirates.
Three days later, a Kyrgyz news site published a notice that Kyrgyzstan had established a new space monitoring center to receive, process, and utilize data transmitted from the newly launched Altair satellite. 
This was striking for two reasons. First, the name “Altair” had been missing from earlier government press releases. Second – and more importantly – it said the monitoring center would be “provided” data coming from the “UAE-operated” satellite by a body called the Abu Dhabi Maritime Academy. 
Suddenly, Japarov’s claims that Kyrgyzstan would be “no longer dependent” on other countries began to ring hollow.
Not only had Russian technology supposedly been used to design the satellite, but the UAE was apparently going to operate the craft, with Kyrgyzstan merely receiving “access” to its data.
It also didn’t help that Gulf-focused news sites were calling Altair the “first satellite developed and built by UAE engineers,” without even mentioning Bishkek’s involvement in the project.  
What, then, had happened on October 1? Had Kyrgyzstan really launched a satellite of its own making? If so, in what ways were other countries involved? And if the craft launched from California was primarily an Emirati initiative, would Bishkek walk back its claims of national self-sufficiency? 
So far, none of the above questions have been definitively answered. And the matter, described by one prominent regional commentator as a “scandal of cosmic proportions,” has prompted a growing number of increasingly conspiratorial explanations. 
Local news outlet Kaktus Media, for example, suggested that two satellites were likely launched on October 1, one developed by the UAE and one with Russian assistance. (It also noted that Kyrgyzstan’s first satellite initiative, launched in 2019 by a team of all-female engineers, seemed not to be involved, having been wound down previously with no details about the project’s completion.)
Tandyr Media, meanwhile, an independent media outlet known for its popular YouTube channel, drew attention in its video covering the launch to a series of Threads posts by an individual named Dima Balakirev, who claimed to have been personally involved in the satellite project’s development.
In his post, Balakirev appeared to depict himself standing next to a different — much larger — satellite than had been shown in the government’s earlier press releases. Incidentally, the photo also clearly showed a line of text reading “Made in UAE” on one side of the satellite.
According to Balakirev, the spacecraft was a joint project with the UAE, entirely funded “by grants and the Abu Dhabi government,” and was an Earth Remote Sensing satellite – that is, likely the satellite that Japarov was referring to when he was talking about Kyrgyzstan’s newfound capacity to survey itself from above. (Subsequent reporting from government-affiliated sources mentioning the Altair satellite likewise suggested that its data would be used in agricultural planning, water resource management, and environmental monitoring.)
Notably, when questioned by Threads users citing the government’s original (smaller) size specifications, Balakirev insisted that national news outlets had confused two different projects:
“The first is a satellite for Kyrgyzstan, which was assembled in Abu Dhabi. This is a joint project with the UAE, and the Emirates are covering the entire cost. The second is a satellite being built by the team at Kyrgyz Electronics. This is a separate project with its own objectives. The figure of 5 kg and 10–12 million soms [$114,350 – $137,200] refers specifically to this one.” 
Although Balakirev’s exact title and position are unknown, as Tandyr Media pointed out, the self-described “entrepreneur and techie” appeared to have been present in California alongside Japarov, and shared Instagram stories from the event. 
Given all that, as Tandyr host Dmitriy Lozhnikov himself concluded, what is left now is a substantially muddied picture. 
According to one possible version of events, Kyrgyzstan did launch its smaller, unnamed bread-loaf-sized satellite, whose function is not entirely clear, on October 1. On the same day, meanwhile, the larger, UAE-designed Altair satellite also launched from California – data from which Bishkek has confirmed it is now paying to access.
In another plausible version, proposed by emigre political scientist Aidarbek Raev, the Kyrgyz-designed nanosatellite might not have been launched at all, which would mean that reports of Kyrgyzstan’s national technological achievements have been greatly exaggerated.
articles.summary: At first glance, the story of Kyrgyzstan’s satellite launch seemed like a genuine achievement. Then the story changed.

articles.title: South Korea Recalls Ambassador, Demands Public Apology From Ukraine
articles.full_text:
A diplomatic rift is growing after a North Korean prisoner transfer that Kyiv revealed against Seoul’s wishes.
South Korea decided on October 8 to recall Ambassador Park Ki-chang from Ukraine. It’s Seoul’s first ambassador recall since 2008, when South Korea withdrew its envoy from Japan over a territorial claim to the Dokdo islets. 
The decision came 15 days after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of two captured North Korean soldiers to South Korea in a speech to the United Nations General Assembly. Seoul says the two governments had agreed to keep the transfer confidential. However, Kyiv first denied any such agreement before its Foreign Ministry attributed the dispute to differing interpretations.
The two soldiers at the center of the dispute were captured in January 2025 in the Kursk region of Russia. North Korea had sent troops there to support the Russian invasion of Ukraine. The captured soldiers arrived in South Korea in mid-September after saying they wished to settle there.
Zelenskyy’s public announcement of their arrival drew a response from South Korean President Lee Jae-myung on September 24 in a post on the social platform X. He called the disclosure deeply regrettable. Lee also cited the problems that disclosure could cause.
Kyiv rejected that account the next day. Dmytro Lytvyn, a communications adviser to Zelenskyy, denied that any confidentiality agreement existed.
The South Korean presidential office voiced strong regret over the disclosure and Ukraine’s denial on September 27. It demanded an official explanation and apology. It also signaled that additional measures were under consideration. Seong Ghi-hong, senior presidential secretary for public relations, said that Ukraine’s had sought the secrecy itself. He added that Kyiv had cited possible criticism at home for giving up a chance to swap the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners held by Russia.
The next day, First Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo summoned Andrii Vieshkin, who is Ukraine’s acting ambassador in Seoul. The vice minister repeated the demands to him.
Still, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the dispute on October 1 as a diplomatic misunderstanding. Sybiha did not offer the public apology that Seoul had demanded.
In a post on X the next day, Lee wrote that Ukraine had made the South Korean head of state a “liar” by denying the agreement. He also warned of further measures unless Kyiv publicly apologized.
Lee also broadened his criticism to remarks by Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian presidential office. Budanov had warned in an interview on September 27 that tension along the inter-Korean border was rising by the day. Days earlier, suspected North Korean mines had exploded inside the Demilitarized Zone between the two Koreas and wounded three South Korean soldiers. So Lee accused Kyiv of speaking of an imminent clash between the two Koreas as if wishing for war. 
On October 6, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun told lawmakers that a message from Ukraine had included words of apology. However, he said it fell somewhat short of the expectations of Seoul.
Kyiv characterized the message differently. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said on October 7 that Ukraine had expressed regret over the public criticism between the two countries. The spokesperson also attributed the dispute to differing interpretations of the confidentiality arrangement.
A separate dispute surfaced in the same week. Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the presidential commissioner of Ukraine for sanctions policy, said on October 6 that fuel shipments from South Korean ports had helped Russia offset refinery losses caused by Ukrainian strikes. The South Korean presidential office rejected the claim on October 7.
In the announcement recalling Ambassador Park the next day, the South’s Foreign Ministry said it hoped to settle pending issues through continued consultations with Ukraine.
The Foreign Ministry of Ukraine responded that diplomacy should prevail over emotions. Tykhyi added that diplomatic efforts were underway through private channels. 
Seoul had good reasons to want the transfer kept quiet. According to Seoul, the families of the two men remain in North Korea, where they could face reprisals over their relatives’ decision to defect. 
The National Intelligence Service also told lawmakers on September 30 that the disclosure appeared aimed at building public support in South Korea for arms supplies to Ukraine. Seoul has supported Ukraine with financial and humanitarian aid but not with lethal weapons, even after North Korea began sending tens of thousands of soldiers to fight for Russia.
If Ukraine’s government was hoping to bolster its image with South Koreans, it badly miscalculated. Instead, Kyiv has lost the trust of Seoul, and the harm cannot be repaired in private. Because the disclosure was public, a message passed between ministers cannot solve the problem. 
Meanwhile another Ukrainian official opened a second dispute. Vlasiuk raised the fuel claim on October 6 while Seoul was still waiting for an apology. The South Korean government says petroleum products are not on its list of controlled exports. Whatever the merits, the claim muddied a dispute that Kyiv had started. The fuel question belongs in a separate channel on sanctions compliance.
With that question set aside, Seoul has demanded three things. Kyiv should acknowledge that a confidentiality agreement existed. The Ukrainian government should offer an official, public apology. And Kyiv should commit to steps that prevent a recurrence. 
Park may return to Kyiv only after Ukraine does all three.
